title: How Prayer Healing Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss whether prayer has measurable health effects. They cover studies finding people who pray tend to have lower blood pressure, slower heart rates and longer lives, with lifestyle confounders considered. The main focus is intercessory (distant) prayer: Randolph Bird's 1988 study of heart patients prayed for by groups, which reported a large recovery difference (about 85 percent versus 73.1 percent), and the STEP study (Study of the Effects of Intercessory Prayer), published in the American Heart Journal, which found no benefit and worse outcomes among patients who knew they were being prayed for. They discuss the difficulty of controlling prayer as a variable, and the debate among scientists and religious believers over studying prayer. They close with a plug for a HowStuffWorks article on hidden passageways.

segments.title: Opening banter and listener mail correction
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the show, joke about a listener mistaking Josh's name for Brian, and transition to the topic of intercessory prayer. A sponsor read for GoToMyPC appears at the start.

segments.title: Prayer and healthier lives
segments.summary: Discussion of studies showing people who pray or meditate tend to have lower blood pressure, slower heart rates and longer lives. Lifestyle factors like avoiding alcohol and smoking are raised as an explanation, and follow-up studies that controlled for them still found differences. Chuck offers a meditation-based theory.

segments.title: Intercessory prayer defined
segments.summary: The hosts explain intercessory or distant prayer, praying on behalf of someone who is sick, and describe congregational prayer lists as a familiar practice.

segments.title: Randolph Bird study
segments.summary: Josh describes Randolph Bird's 1988 study of about 353 matched heart patients, prayed for by Christian groups in California while a control group was not. Reported recovery rates were about 85 percent for the prayed-for group versus 73.1 percent for the control. Josh calls it a landmark study that used the scientific method and was never overturned.

segments.title: STEP study and contradictory results
segments.summary: The STEP study (Study of the Effects of Intercessory Prayer), published in the American Heart Journal across six US medical centers, split patients into three groups. Those who were prayed for without knowing had recovery similar to those not prayed for, and patients who knew they were being prayed for had the worst outcomes, with 50 having complications after heart surgery. The hosts note this contradicts the Bird study.

segments.title: Difficulties and debate over studying prayer
segments.summary: Hosts discuss why prayer is hard to control in studies, including patients praying for themselves and others praying, and the difficulty of standardizing prayer. Prayer is noted as a top alternative medicine in America. They discuss skeptics and religious believers who oppose studying it, and conclude the jury is still out.

segments.title: Sign-off and HowStuffWorks plug
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up with a personal take on prayer, then Chuck previews an article on installing hidden passageways in homes, with a HowStuffWorks plug and sponsor read.
